Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA comer Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 43 s. 2023 HON. ANTONIO O. BENDITA Vice Mayor Municipality of Surallah South Cotabato Dear Vice-Mayor Bendita: This refers to your letter-request dated March 6, 2023, requesting this Department's opinion concerning Municipal Appropriation Ordinance No. 3, series of 2022. As represented in the subject letter, hereunder are the pertinent factual antecedents: • The Municipal Appropriation Ordinance No. 3 (Annual Budget FY 2023) of Surallah, Province of South Cotabato, was cut down by the Sangguniang Bayan due to questions regarding the budget allocation of certain offices, in particular the Confidential Fund of the Office of the Municipal Mayor. On December 23, 2023, the sanggunian approved the said ordinance. On January 10, 2023, it was subsequently submitted to the Office of the Municipal Mayor for approval. On January 19, 2023, the said ordinance was submitted back to the sanggunian with the attached Direct Item Veto Message from the Municipal Mayor. The Direct Item Veto Message included items in the Annual Budget, in particular the Confidential Fund of the Office of the Municipal Mayor, which was cut down by the sanggunian to zero pesos (Php 0.00). On January 23, 2023, Vice Mayor Bendita instructed the SB Secretary to submit the subject ordinance to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan while copies of the Veto Message were withheld to be tackled separately for deliberation and action in the plenary. On February 14, 2023, copies of the Veto Message were subsequently submitted to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan for their information and reference. Apparently, while the said matter is under Second Reading, it became known to the sanggunian, through the appearance of the members of the Local Finance Committee of Surallah in its Regular Session dated March 3, 2023, that the Confidential Fund amounting to Php 2.5 million was released on February 15, 2023 through a Memorandum Order issued by the Office of the Mayor to the Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

concerned offices. The sanggunian did not receive a copy of the said Memorandum Order. Premised from the foregoing, arose the following issues for this Department's legal opinion, thus: 1. Was the Sangguniang Bayan of Surallah justified in its decision to submit the subject Appropriation Ordinance given that the same was signed on all pages, even if there are vetoed items (Line-Item Veto) by the Municipal Mayor? 2. Can the Veto Message of the Municipal Mayor be deliberated by the sanggunian even if the Annual Budget [has already been] submitted to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan? 3. Does the Executive Department have the power to release the budget for the Confidential Fund of the Municipal Mayor, considering that the matter (vetoed item) is still being deliberated by the sanggunian? and 4. Did the Executive Department overstep its boundaries by authorizing the release of the Confidential Fund without consulting with the sanggunian, given that the matter is still being deliberated in the plenary? At the outset, attention is respectfully directed to pertinent provisions of the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160, hereinafter referred to as the "Code"), which govern the dynamics of the approval of local ordinances, thus: "Section 319. Legislative Authorization of the Budget. — On or before the end of the current fiscal year, the sanggunian concerned shall enact, through an ordinance, the annual budget of the local government unit for the ensuing fiscal year on the basis of the estimates of income and expenditures submitted by the local chief executive." Section 54. Approval of Ordinances. - (a) Every ordinance enacted by the sangguniang panlalawigan, sangguniang panlungsod, or sangguniang bayan shall be presented to the provincial governor or city or municipal mayor, as the case may be. If the local chief executive concerned approves the same, he shall affix his signature on each and every page thereof; otherwise, he shall veto it and return the same with his objections to the sanggunian, which may proceed to reconsider the same. The sanggunian concerned may override the veto of the local chief executive by two-thirds (2/3) vote of all its members, thereby making the ordinance or resolution effective for all legal intents and purposes. (b) The veto shall be communicated by the local chief executive concerned to the sanggunian within fifteen (15) days in the case of a province, and ten (IO) days in the case of a city or a municipality; otherwise, the ordinance shall be deemed approved as if he had signed it. (c) xxx Page 2 of 2

Section 55. Veto Power of the Local Chief Executive. - (a) The local chief executive may veto any ordinance of the sanggunian panlalawigan, sangguniang panlungsod, or sanggunian bayan on the ground that it is ultra vires or prejudicial to the public welfare, stating his reasons therefor in writing. (b) The local chief executive, except the punong barangay, shall have the power to veto any particular item or items of an appropriations ordinance, an ordinance or resolution adopting a local development plan and public investment program, or an ordinance directing the payment of money or creating liability. In such a case, the veto shall not affect the item or items which are not objected to. The vetoed item or items shall not take effect unless the sanggunian overrides the veto in the manner herein provided; otherwise, the item or items in the appropriations ordinance of the previous year corresponding to those vetoed, if any, shall be deemed reenacted. (c) The local chief executive may veto an ordinance or resolution only once. The sanggunian may override the veto of the local chief executive concerned by two-thirds (2/3) vote of all its members, thereby making the ordinance effective even without the approval of the local chief executive concerned." (Emphasis supplied) Section 319 of the Code, as above-cited, is rather clear that the sanggunian—in the herein case, Sangguniang Bayan—shall enact, through an ordinance, the annual budget of the sanggunian for the ensuing fiscal year on the basis of the estimates of income and expenditures submitted by the local chief executive. The legislative instrument authorizing the budget is known as an Appropriation Ordinance. Section 54 details the procedure vis-å-vis the approval of such an ordinance. Ordinances enacted by the sanggunian shall be presented to the local chief executive for his consideration. Now, if the local chief executive approves the same, he shall affix his signature on each page thereof; otherwise, he shall veto it and return the same with his objections to the sanggunian, which may proceed to reconsider the same. A veto is defined as the refusal of assent by the executive officer whose assent is necessary to perfect a law which has been passed by the legislative body and the message which is usually sent to such body by the executive, stating such refusal and the reasons therefor (Black's Law Dictionary, 5th Ed., 1983). Section 55 (b) of the Code authorizes the local chief executive—in the herein case, the municipal mayor—to veto any particular item or items of an appropriation ordinance. In such a case, the veto shall not affect the item or items that are not objected to. It should be emphasized that the item vetoed by the local chief executive should be made in writing so that the sanggunian concerned may properly consider it and decide whether to override it or not. The overriding power is accorded to the sanggunian as part of the checks and balances between the legislative and executive branches and, at the same time, as a remedy for the sanggunian to give effect to those items previously vetoed by the local chief executive. The manner in which the sanggunian may exercise its overriding power is laid down under the aforequoted Section 55 (c), which provides that if the Page 2 of 3

sanggunian shall override the veto of the local chief executive, the same may be done by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of all its members, thereby making the ordinance effective even without the approval of the local chief executive concerned. Once overridden by the sanggunian, the vetoed ordinance or any item thereof shall no longer be presented to the local chief executive for approval as it already becomes deemed approved by operation of law, even without the approval of the latter. On the other hand, if the sanggunian fails to override the veto, the item(s) in the appropriations ordinance of the previous year corresponding to those vetoed, if any, shall be deemed reenacted (DILG Legal Opinion No. 30 series of 2008, dated May 8, 2008). Having laid down the foregoing discussions, we shall now address the foregoing query squarely. We deemed it apt to address the first and second issues in one discussion since they are both fundamentally interrelated. This level submits that the act of the sanggunian in submitting its annual budget to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan despite the vetoed item in the appropriation ordinance in question and with the intention of deliberating upon such vetoed items at a later time or after such an ordinance has been submitted to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan is an utter disregard of the procedures provided by the Code. The Code detailed the procedures in the approval of an ordinance, which should be followed systematically. The act of the sanggunian in submitting the appropriation ordinance to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan sans taking into consideration the vetoed items thereof, when they should have instead exercised their veto power, may be deemed to have waived its "overriding power", which implies that the sanggunian has, for all intents and purposes, exercised its legislative authorization of such an appropriation ordinance pursuant to Section 319 of the Code. As to the third issue, we deemed it apt to address it together with the fourth issue as they are likewise interrelated. Here, it should be emphasized that the failure of the sanggunian to exercise its "overriding power", vis-å-vis the vetoed items of the appropriation in question has the effect of reenacting the item on the Confidential Fund in the appropriation ordinance of the previous year as provided under Section 55 (b) of the Code. Nevertheless, it is to be noted that pending review by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of the appropriation ordinance, the same can be validly enforced so that funds corresponding thereto can already be disbursed because the effectivity of an ordinance is not contingent upon the review of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan but rather in accordance with Section 320 of the Code. 1 Accordingly, for failure of the sanggunian to override the veto, the Executive Department did not overstep its boundaries by authorizing the release of the I Section 320. Effectivity of Budgets. - The ordinance enacting the annual budget shall take effect at the beginning of the ensuing calendar year. An ordinance enacting a supplemental budget, however, shall take effect upon its approval or on the date fixed therein. The responsibility for the execution Of the annual and supplemental budgets and the accountability therefor shall be vested primarily in the local chief executive concerned. Page 2 of 4

confidential Fund, taking into consideration the appropriations ordinance of the previous year corresponding to those vetoed, as the same is deemed reenacted. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, B Authority of the Secretary: OR R.
